Choose $0<\varepsilon<r_+/2$ and use the extension manifold $\overline{\mathcal M}:=\mathbb R_v\times(r_+-\varepsilon,\infty)\times S^2$ with its product smooth structure. Let $\bar\pi:\overline{\mathcal M}\to S^2$ be the sphere projection, $\bar\gamma:=\bar\pi^*\gamma_{S^2}$, $\eta:=\bar\pi^*(\gamma_{S^2}(\xi,\cdot))$, and $q:=\bar\gamma(\xi,\xi)=|\xi|_{\bar\gamma}^2$. These are global smooth tensors or functions; on a polar chart of the new sphere factor, $\eta=\sin^2\theta\,d\widetilde\phi$ and $q=\sin^2\theta$. Fix $r_0>r_+$ and define $f(r)=\int_{r_0}^r (s^2+a^2)/\Delta(s)\,ds$ and $h(r)=\int_{r_0}^r a/\Delta(s)\,ds$ on $(r_+,\infty)$. Their integrands are smooth because $\Delta>0$: repeated use of [F7] gives all derivatives of $\Delta^{-1}$, and [F8] handles the polynomial products. [F6] gives $f,h\in C^1$, and successive differentiation of $f'=(r^2+a^2)/\Delta$ and $h'=a/\Delta$ shows that both primitives are smooth. Set $v=t+f(r)$ and, on the sphere factor, replace each point $(x,y,z)$ by $R_{h(r)}(x,y,z):=(x\cos h-y\sin h,x\sin h+y\cos h,z)$. Repeated application of [F10] makes this rotation smoothly dependent on $r$, and its inverse is $R_{-h(r)}$. Thus the exterior map is a smooth diffeomorphism, with coordinate Jacobian determinant $1$ on every polar chart; there $\widetilde\phi=\phi+h(r)$ and the pullback of the original $\xi^\flat$ is $\eta-aq\Delta^{-1}dr$. Substitution in [F1], using $\Sigma^2+a^2q(\Sigma+2Mr)=(r^2+a^2)^2-a^2\Delta q$, gives the global ingoing expression
$$g=-\frac{\Delta-a^2q}{\Sigma}\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+\Sigma\bar\gamma+\frac{a^2(\Sigma+2Mr)}{\Sigma}\eta\otimes\eta-\frac{2aMr}{\Sigma}(dv\otimes\eta+\eta\otimes dv)-a(dr\otimes\eta+\eta\otimes dr).$$
For every $r>r_+-\varepsilon>r_+/2>0$, one has $\Sigma>0$ and $\Delta=A-2Mr<A$, where $A:=r^2+a^2$. If $\Delta\ge0$, then $A^2-a^2\Delta q\ge A^2-a^2\Delta\ge A^2-a^2A=Ar^2>0$; if $\Delta<0$, then $A^2-a^2\Delta q\ge A^2>0$. Consequently the angular restriction in an off-axis polar chart, $\Sigma\,d\theta^2+\frac{q(A^2-a^2\Delta q)}{\Sigma}\,d\widetilde\phi^2$, is positive definite. The determinant of the full metric matrix there is $-\Sigma^2q<0$; its Schur complement in the $(v,r)$ directions is symmetric with negative determinant, hence has one negative and one positive eigenvalue. The full metric therefore has signature $(-,+,+,+)$ off the axis. At an axis point $\eta=0$ and $\Sigma=A$; the $(v,r)$ block has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-\Delta/\Sigma&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ of determinant $-1$, and the sphere block is $\Sigma\gamma_{S^2}$ on the tangent space, so the extension has the same Lorentzian signature there. Every coefficient in the global expression is smooth across $r=r_+$ because $\Sigma>0$ and no coefficient contains $\Delta$ in a denominator. It is a smooth Lorentzian extension across $r=r_+$. In this chart $g^{-1}(dr,dr)=\Delta/\Sigma$, so $dr(\sharp_gdr)=g^{-1}(dr,dr)=0$ on $H^+$ by [F9]; the normal is null and tangent there. [A1, F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

Apply [F8] to the positive scaling $\eta\mapsto\xi=\epsilon\eta$, whose Jacobian is $\epsilon^d$, to obtain the substitution $\eta=\xi/\epsilon$ and $d\xi=\epsilon^d d\eta$. Write $\widehat f_x(\eta)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}f_x(y)\,dy$, the rescaled negative-sign $2\pi$ transform. Then $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi)^{-d}\int\widehat{f_x}(\eta)\,d\eta=f_x(0)=|u(x)|^2, $$ where the middle equality follows from [F4] at zero after the change from the library frequency $\eta/(2\pi)$ to $\eta$, also covered by [F8]. All integrals are absolutely convergent because $f_x,\widehat{f_x}\in\mathcal S$. [given, A1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

mapping.current_paragraph: On $M_d(\mathbb C)$ define $\mathcal N(X)=KX+XK^*$, $\mathcal J(X)=\sum_aL_aXL_a^*$, and $\mathcal T_u=e^{u\mathcal L}$. By [F5], these finite sums of left and right matrix multiplications are bounded in trace norm. Expanding [F1] gives $\mathcal L=\mathcal N+\mathcal J$. Fix $t>0$. Integrate finite-dimensional matrix and superoperator entries by their real and imaginary components, using the repeated Riemann convention in [F2]. The curve $s\mapsto e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal T_s$ has continuously differentiable entries by [F4]; its real and imaginary derivative components are continuous and hence integrable by [F8]. Differentiation gives $\frac{d}{ds}(e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal T_s)=e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\mathcal T_s$, since $\mathcal L=\mathcal N+\mathcal J$. Applying [F9] entrywise yields $\mathcal T_t=e^{t\mathcal N}+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\mathcal T_s\,ds$. This finite identity follows by induction on $N$: the base case is the displayed variation-of-constants identity, and substituting that identity for the final $\mathcal T_{s_1}$ in the remainder adds the next ordered-simplex term and a remainder with one more innermost time. Only finite linearity of the nested integrals is used; no integration order is exchanged. Thus, for each $N\geq0$, $\mathcal T_t=\sum_{n=0}^{N}S_n(t)+Q_{N+1}(t)$, where $S_0(t)=e^{t\mathcal N}$, $S_n(t)=\int_{0<s_1<\cdots<s_n<t}e^{(t-s_n)\mathcal N}\mathcal J e^{(s_n-s_{n-1})\mathcal N}\cdots\mathcal J e^{s_1\mathcal N}\,d\mathbf s$ for $n\geq1$, and $Q_m(t)=\int_{0<s_1<\cdots<s_m<t}e^{(t-s_m)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\bigl(\prod_{j=m-1,\ldots,1}e^{(s_{j+1}-s_j)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\bigr)\mathcal T_{s_1}\,d\mathbf s$ for $m=N+1$, where the product is ordered from left to right with descending $j$, and the empty product is the identity. For $m=1$ the intermediate exponential factors are absent: $Q_1(t)=\int_0^t e^{(t-s_1)\mathcal N}\mathcal J\mathcal T_{s_1}\,ds_1$, exactly the displayed variation-of-constants remainder. In particular there is no extra $e^{s_1\mathcal N}$ before $\mathcal T_{s_1}$. All these integrands are continuous in finite-dimensional coordinates on the closed ordered simplex; [F11] proves that every inner integral is continuous in its remaining parameters and hence the full repeated integral exists. The insertion of one further nested integral in the induction is therefore legitimate. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F8, F9, F11, algebra]

If $E$ is the spectral measure of $B$, then $F(\Lambda):=C^{-1}E(\Lambda)C$ is a spectral measure of orthogonal projections on $H$, and its spectral integral is $P$; hence $P$ is positive self-adjoint. The operator $J$ is antilinear, vanishes on $\ker T$, and is isometric on $(\ker T)^\perp$, since $C$ maps $\ker T$ onto $\ker A$ and preserves orthogonality.
